opus-5.5.text:
I think it's helpful to remember how CUDA looked from the inside at the beginning. When NVIDIA started investing in it, around 2006, there was no obvious market waiting for general-purpose GPU computing. GPUs were for graphics, for games. Spending large amounts of engineering effort so that scientists, a few researchers, maybe some people doing physics simulations could program the GPU looked, to many outside observers, like a distraction. For years it didn't produce meaningful revenue, and Wall Street questioned it.

So the risk was real. But how Jensen and the company thought about it was less "is there a market today?" and more "is this a fundamentally better way to compute, and if so, will the world eventually need it?" The belief was that accelerated computing, parallel computing, would matter for a very wide range of problems. If you believe that, you have to build the platform before the killer application shows up, because the application can't appear without the platform. Nobody writes the software if there's no programming model, no libraries, no developer community.

There's also a point about patience and consistency. A lot of companies take a bet, and if it doesn't pay off in two or three years, they cut it. NVIDIA kept CUDA compatible across every generation of GPU, even consumer gaming cards. That meant any student with a gaming laptop could experiment. That decision cost money and effort, but it built an enormous installed base. When deep learning arrived, with AlexNet in 2012 trained on GPUs, the ecosystem was already there. It looked like luck from the outside, but it was preparation meeting an opportunity.

As a researcher, I see a parallel with how we think about research. Most of the important directions look risky or even unreasonable at first. If something is obviously a good idea, many people are already doing it, and your advantage is small. Real long-term value often comes from investing early in something you deeply believe in, and then sticking with it long enough for the world to catch up.

Of course, not every bet works. The company has made bets that didn't pan out. But the culture tolerates that, as long as the reasoning was sound and you learn quickly. For me, the lesson of CUDA is less about one lucky bet and more about having a first-principles conviction, being willing to pay for it for a long time, and building the whole stack, hardware, software, and community, so that when the moment comes you're ready.

r001.rationale: The response discusses CUDA’s engineering cost and ecosystem benefits, but does not attribute NVIDIA GPUs’ higher price for the same FLOPs to supporting CUDA programmability.

r002.rationale: It calls the CUDA investment a real risk and explains why NVIDIA pursued it, but does not judge that foregoing such an investment would be riskier.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that skipping CUDA-like investments would gradually turn NVIDIA’s products into commodities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the way Jensen thinks about it, and the way the company has always thought about it, is a little different from how most people frame risk. CUDA, when it started around 2006, 2007, was not a sure thing. You're building a programming model for a GPU, and at that time most people saw GPUs as graphics chips for gaming. Investing a lot of engineering effort into making them general-purpose, and keeping that investment going for years before there's an obvious market, that looks very risky from the outside.

But internally, the logic was more about belief in a direction. If you believe that accelerated computing is where computation needs to go, because the CPU's performance scaling is slowing down, then not investing is actually the bigger risk. You'd be betting that the world stays the way it is. So the question becomes less "what if this fails" and more "how do we make sure we're ready when the moment comes." And honestly, nobody knew the moment would be deep learning. When AlexNet happened in 2012, that was kind of a gift. The platform was already there, researchers could just pick it up.

What I've seen from inside, in research especially, is that the company is comfortable with long time horizons. We work on things where there's no product in sight for several years. The leadership is willing to put resources behind that, with the expectation that some of it won't pan out. That tolerance is really the core of it. You accept that a lot of bets lose, but you want to be positioned so that when one of them hits, you've already built the whole ecosystem, the tools, the libraries, the developer community, and you're years ahead.

So I'd say the risk is real, but it's a deliberate kind of risk. It's not gambling. It's committing to a thesis about where computing goes and then being patient enough to let the world catch up.

astra-6.text:
I think the risk is that you have to invest long before you know whether the market will be there. With something like CUDA, building the technology is only part of the challenge. You also need developers to learn it, build tools around it, and find problems where it provides enough value to change how they work. That takes time, and the payoff is uncertain.

But there’s also a risk in waiting until the opportunity is obvious. By then, you haven’t built the tools or the ecosystem you need. So I think about it as making a long-term bet on a technical direction, while continuing to learn from what people actually do with it. You need conviction to sustain that investment, but also the willingness to adjust as you learn.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention NVIDIA GPUs’ price or attribute it to supporting CUDA programmability.

r002.rationale: It notes that waiting carries risks, but does not judge that foregoing CUDA is riskier than pursuing it.

r003.rationale: The response does not say NVIDIA’s products would gradually become commodities without investments like CUDA.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the risk is that you have to invest long before you know whether the market will be there. With something like CUDA, you’re building more than a feature. You need the software, the tools, and developers who are willing to learn how to use them. That takes a sustained commitment, and the return may not be obvious for quite a while.

But those investments can also create possibilities you couldn’t fully predict at the beginning. Once researchers can experiment on the platform, they discover new applications, and those applications give you a reason to keep improving it. So I would frame it as a long-term bet: you need conviction about the direction, while staying willing to learn from what people actually do with the technology.
